Transcript body:
[00:00] Jordan (AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Jordan from Redwood, AE on this account. With me is Priya, our solutions engineer. How's everyone doing?
[00:12] Liam (Head of Search): Hey Jordan, thanks. Doing good. We want to figure out what "where to serve" looks like for our embeddings + rerank. We have spikes during promo windows and also strict data residency.
[00:23] Priya (SE): Great, thanks Liam. Can you give us a bit of context — current stack for similarity and reranking, what vector DB and embedding model you use today?
[00:34] Marisol (ML Eng): Right now we push 768-dim embeddings from an in-house encoder and store vectors in a managed service (they said "Pinecone" but sometimes the name comes out wrong on our infra notes). We do a two-step: retrieve top 200 nearest neighbors then rerank with a small LLM reranker. Peak QPS on search is about 220 qps and during promos it spiky to 1.2k QPS for short bursts.
[00:55] Tom (Infra): We also have a VPC and prefer not to send customer PII to a shared multi-tenant endpoint, that's why we're considering Dedicated or Private. SOC2 is required, and we need KMS-backed encryption and audit logs.
[01:12] Jordan (AE): Totally makes sense. From Redwood's side we support Hosted (multi-tenant), Dedicated (reserved GPU pools), and Private (VPC/on-prem options). We can run your rerank and embeddings on-hosted for low lift but if you need isolation and KMS we'd recommend Dedicated or Private.
[01:28] Liam: Can you walk through the economics and the throughput math? For example, if we do fanout 200 and rerank top 50, what's the token cost and latency like?
[01:37] Priya: Sure. There are two cost/latency buckets — vector lookup (kNN) and LLM rerank. Vector DB is mostly I/O and memory bound; we see sub-10ms lookups for small k on high-performance managed stores like Pinecone if index fits in RAM. Fanout 200 multiplies storage read work and network hops. Rerank is an LLM generation call — depending on model size and quantization, that could be 80–250ms per request per candidate if you naively call for each candidate, so typical pattern is retrieve top N (say 200) then run a single batched reranker or a small cross-encoder that scores candidates in one pass to reduce calls.
[02:12] Marisol: We currently do a cross-encoder style rerank but it batches 32 at a time. We were thinking about switching to a lightweight ensemble for performance.
[02:22] Priya: That's an important signal. For throughput math: 220 steady qps * fanout 200 = 44k candidate vectors/sec of read IO. That's heavy if all reads go to the DB; you want caching and sharding. Redwood has automatic prefix/KV caching to cut repeated popular prefixes and continuous batching to improve throughput on inference side. If you hit promo spikes to 1.2k QPS with same fanout, you get 240k vectors/sec unless you reduce fanout for cold/cheap requests.
[02:51] Tom: So caching looks attractive. But for the vector store, we use a managed index and replication. If we instead put embeddings on Dedicated Redwood instances is the idea we do rerank and embedding generation close to where the DB is?
[03:05] Jordan: Two patterns: 1) Keep vector DB managed (Pinecone/Milvus) and route rerank to Redwood Hosted/Dedicated — we support low-latency private peering to some managed stores. 2) Use Redwood Dedicated or Private and co-locate an open-source vector DB (Milvus or Qdrant) on the same VPC — i.e., private deployment where we run the whole stack closer to your data and maintain isolation. Both are viable — trade-offs are operational ownership (you run DB in path) vs convenience.
[03:29] Liam: For dimensions: our research shows 384 is almost as good as 768 for product similarity, and 1536 gives marginal gains but costs more. What's Redwood's guidance?
[03:39] Priya: Right — embedding dimension affects storage, CPU/GPU cost for nearest neighbor ops, and downstream reranker behavior. Higher dims mean larger vectors stored and more memory per shard. For throughput-heavy workloads we often recommend 384 or 512 for the retrieval stage and keep a richer representation for rerank if needed. There is also the option to quantize vectors for storage (e.g., PQ, OPQ, 8-bit) which reduces storage but can change recall. Redwood Optimize can suggest quantization profiles by workload.
[04:07] Marisol: We also want to understand tail latency SLOs. We need 95th < 120ms for lookup + rerank ideally for non-personalized queries. Is that realistic?
[04:18] Priya: 95th < 120ms is aggressive for a full rerank if it includes an LLM generation step. But for cross-encoder style rerank batched correctly and with model quantization, it's possible in Dedicated/private where GPU is dedicated. Hosted can hit similar numbers but at higher cost and with potential noisy neighbors unless you go Dedicated. For pure kNN lookup (no rerank), sub-50ms 95th is achievable on well-provisioned vector stores.
[04:45] Jordan: Also consider hybrid search: use inverted-index recall for cheap filtering, then embed fwd nearest neighbor for the remainder — that reduces fanout. People build a cheap lexical filter or product-category filter to reduce vectors touched per query.
[04:58] Liam: That so-called hybrid top-k routing — we want to keep high recall while lowering fanout. Any tooling Redwood provides to help pick thresholds?
[05:07] Priya: Redwood Optimize includes recommendations: threshold suggestions, batching profiles, and which model/quantization combos to use. We also run offline evals against your query set to simulate cost/latency tradeoffs.
[05:18] Tom: On security: we need KMS-backed key management, audit logs retained for a year, and SAML SSO. Can Redwood support HSM or customer KMS?
[05:29] Jordan: Yes. Dedicated and Private options integrate with customer KMS and HSM in private deployments; Hosted supports customer-managed keys via our KMS integrations in certain regions. We have SOC2 Type II. We'll send over the security pack.
[05:40] Marisol: Good. For the pilot, we want to test 100k vectors then scale to 1M. What's the suggested ramp?
[05:48] Priya: Typical pilot is 100k vectors micro-benchmark for correctness + perf, then move to 500k–1M to test sharding and tail behavior. The micro-benchmark runs: 1) embedding + index ingest 2) kNN retrieval latency under steady and burst 3) rerank end-to-end latency and cost. We'll provide scripts.
[06:03] Liam: For ingestion: we want near-line updates. Our catalog updates every 5 minutes. Does Redwood need a full reindex for small updates?
[06:12] Priya: No, we support incremental upserts. Dedicated/private can do very fast upserts; managed vector stores vary. If you need low-latency nearline updates, co-locating DB on Dedicated/Private helps.
[06:22] Tom: Ok. Cost question — reserved Dedicated seats vs hosted per token. How do you recommend negotiating?
[06:29] Jordan: If you have steady predictable baseline, Dedicated reserved capacity is usually cheaper per request and avoids noisy neighbor issues. For big seasonal spikes, we provide autoscale and burst capacity on Dedicated. Hosted is best if you want minimal ops and smaller scale. Private is for compliance-sensitive customers who need VPC/on-prem control; costs include deployment and support fees. We'll map your usage patterns to a pricing model in the SOW.
[06:48] Marisol: Any notes on quantized model quality for rerank? We worry int8/int4 might mis-rank in edge cases.
[06:55] Priya: Yes — quantization can subtly change scores. For rerank where precision matters, we usually recommend testing quantized models in offline evals; often int8 is safe for many cross-encoders, int4 can be a good tradeoff but needs validation. Redwood Optimize will flag regressions against your eval prompts.
[07:12] Liam: We heard Redwood has prefix/KV caching—does that also cache embedding results?
[07:18] Jordan: We cache frequent queries and prefixes; for embedding generation, we cache identical inputs to avoid duplicate model calls. For vector lookups we implement hot-vector caching (if same vectors are requested frequently) and client-side CDN strategies for static results.
[07:30] Tom: Networking: what's the best path for minimal latency between our VPC and Redwood Dedicated? Private peering or egress?
[07:38] Priya: Private peering (Direct Connect / FastConnect equivalents) gives the best deterministic latency. VPC peering plus allowed IP ranges also works. We'll share a list of recommended network architectures for low-latency rerank traffic.
[07:49] Jordan: Quick interruption — I want to propose a pilot plan: 2-week smoke: 100k vectors, run retrieval + rerank microbench, validate 95/99th latencies and cost. If that looks good, 4-week scale test to 1M vectors with Dedicated capacity sizing. Thoughts?
[08:03] Liam: Sounds reasonable. We need to align on pass/fail criteria though — e.g., 95th < 200ms with rerank, cost per query < $0.00X (they didn't want to say exact on call).
[08:13] Marisol: Also will need an eval set to measure relevance — we'll share three utility queries sets we care most about and ground truth labels for top 10.
[08:21] Priya: Perfect. We'll run offline evals and send an A/B bench. We'll also attempt a hybrid approach to reduce fanout and show cost savings.
[08:30] Liam: On DB choice — we like Pinecone managed but are curious about self-hosting Milvus on Dedicated. Pros/cons?
[08:37] Priya: Pinecone is convenient, managed, and often great performance. Self-hosted Milvus/Qdrant gives you control, custom index types (IVF, HNSW) and can be cheaper at scale but requires ops. Redwood can operate co-located DB on Private deployments if you want us to manage it.
[08:51] Tom: For logging and audit — we must have request-level audit logs and ability to pull export for compliance.
[08:57] Jordan: Yes, Dedicated/Private give you full audit logs; Hosted provides aggregated logs but we can surface request-level logs controlled by retention policies as an add-on.
[09:08] Marisol: Are there hard limits on embedding dim or shard size in Redwood's runtimes?
[09:14] Priya: No hard limit, but practical guidance: for high-throughput nearest neighbor search you want smaller dims to reduce memory. We typically see 512/768 as sweet spots. Shard sizes and GPU memory set how many vectors stay hot in memory—if you have high qps and large dims, you'll need more replicas.
[09:29] Liam: Could you summarize recommended architecture for our constraints?
[09:33] Priya: Briefly: 1) Hybrid filter + 384–512-dim retrieval embeddings to reduce fanout. 2) Use cross-encoder rerank batched and quantized on Dedicated GPU to hit latency targets. 3) Use caching for hot prefixes and incremental upserts for frequent catalog churn. 4) Start pilot with managed vector DB (Pinecone) for speed, then evaluate moving to co-located Milvus on Dedicated if cost or control requires it.
[09:59] Tom: That aligns. One more: SAML integration and role-based access — we want RBAC for model deployments.
[10:05] Jordan: We support SAML/SSO and RBAC. We'll share docs and how we map roles to Console permissions.
[10:12] Liam: Anything about fallback strategies when Dedicated runs out of capacity during a promo?
[10:18] Priya: We have smart routing and fallbacks — policy-based routing to a smaller cheaper hosted model, or degrade to lexical-only results for a configurable percent of traffic. We'll demo routing policies in the Console.
[10:30] Marisol: Good to hear. Ok, let's talk timeline logistics for the pilot checklist.
[10:34] Jordan: We'll send a SOW + pilot pricing by next Tuesday 2029-07-22. Priya will send benchmark scripts and an adoption checklist.
[10:41] Marisol: We'll get you the query sets and 1k doc subset by 2029-07-24. Tom will share firewall/VPC rules by 2029-07-23.
[10:49] Liam: Any blockers from Redwood side for starting the smoke test quickly?
[10:54] Priya: No blockers — we just need the dataset and access pattern details; if you choose Private we'll need a short security call to map KMS/HSM and network.
[11:03] Jordan: Cool. Closing recap: pilot, security follow-up, SOW and scripts. Anything else?
[11:08] Tom: Nothing from infra — appreciate the network doc.
[11:11] Marisol: Thanks — excited to see the microbench numbers.
[11:14] Liam: Thanks all.
[11:17] Jordan: Thanks everyone — we'll follow up.
[11:20] (call ends)
